# What HDF5 is {#sec-overview .unnumbered}

HDF5 is a file format for arrays that works like a file system in a file. It
has three concepts (@fig-structure). A group is like a directory: it holds
datasets and other groups, and a path names each, such as
`/run_01/temperature`. A dataset is HDF5's name for an array: values of one
type with any number of dimensions, up to 32, such as a vector of 720
latitudes or floats of shape 365 × 720 × 1440 for a year of daily maps of
temperature. The number of dimensions is fixed when the dataset is created. A
dataset is like a file of this file system, but not a file on the disk: all
groups and datasets lie inside the one HDF5 file. Parquet uses the word for a
directory of files instead ([](parquet.qmd#sec-datasets)). An attribute is a
small named value on a group or a dataset, such as the units of a dataset or
the parameters of a run, so that the arrays and what they mean travel
together, in one file that can be copied, archived, and published as it is.

![An HDF5 file, `ocean.h5`, with the results of two runs of an ocean model. The group `/` holds everything in the file: two datasets of coordinates, `lat` and `lon`, and a group for each run, which holds the datasets of the run, shown for `/run_01` only. Each dataset is an array of one type and shape, and each attribute is tied to the group or the dataset it describes.](figures/structure.svg){#fig-structure}

Inside the file, HDF5 usually cuts a dataset into chunks, blocks of its
values, and keeps an index of where each lies. Almost everything that makes
HDF5 fast or fragile follows from the chunks and from the one file, which one
program at a time writes (@sec-storage). Working with it comes down to writing
and reading slices of datasets, and to looking inside files (@sec-usage).

Many formats of the sciences are HDF5 inside, such as NetCDF-4 in the earth
sciences (@sec-netcdf), AnnData (`.h5ad`) in single-cell biology, NeXus at
neutron and X-ray sources, and the MAT-files of MATLAB since version 7.3, so
the tools of this document open them too. In Python, h5py reads and writes
HDF5, in R, the packages rhdf5 of Bioconductor and hdf5r, and HDF5 itself
brings command-line tools, such as `h5ls` and `h5dump`. Tables belong in
[](parquet.qmd) instead, and arrays that many processes write at once, or that
live in the cloud, in [](zarr.qmd).

Checked against HDF5 2.0 with h5py 3.16, the command-line tools of HDF5 1.14,
rhdf5 2.56, and xarray 2026.9.


# How HDF5 stores arrays {#sec-storage}

A chunk is a piece of one dataset: a block of its values. The shape of the
chunks is chosen when the dataset is created: chunks of 1 × 720 × 1440 cut
`temperature` into 365 chunks, the map of one day each. HDF5 stores every
chunk, and compresses it, on its own, somewhere in the file, and an index
inside the file records where each chunk lies. Chunks have no names, paths, or
attributes, and a program never handles them: it reads or writes a slice, such
as the map of one day, and HDF5 finds the chunks that hold it. A dataset may
also be stored contiguously, as one block, but compression and datasets that
grow need chunks.


## Read only the chunks you need {#sec-chunks}

Reading a slice of a dataset reads, and decompresses, every chunk that the
slice touches, and only these. The shape of the chunks so decides which slices
are fast: with a chunk per day, the map of one day is one chunk, but the time
series of one point touches all 365 chunks, nearly the whole dataset. Choose
the shape of the chunks after the slices that are read most often, with a size
of about 100 KB to a few MB: small chunks make the index large, and large
chunks read more than is needed. The shape cannot change afterwards;
`h5repack` copies a file with other chunks (@sec-inspect).


## The order of the axes {#sec-axis-order}

HDF5 stores arrays in row-major order, as C and NumPy do, and lists the axes
from the slowest to the fastest. Languages that store arrays in column-major
order, such as R, Julia, Fortran, and MATLAB, show the same dataset with its
axes reversed: a dataset of shape 365 × 720 × 1440, written with h5py, has the
dimensions 1440 × 720 × 365 in R. The values are the same, but every index is
reversed, and an attribute that names the axes, such as `time`, `lat`, `lon`,
names them in the order of the writer, not of the reader. A square matrix, such
as a matrix of distances, arrives transposed without an error
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-conventions)). Check the order of the axes
in every language that reads a file, or select them by name (@sec-netcdf).


## Attributes and fill values {#sec-attributes}

HDF5 stores attributes but prescribes none: it has no standard for units, for
the names of the axes, or for missing values. Store them anyway, as attributes
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-conventions)), or write NetCDF-4, which
fixes all three (@sec-netcdf). HDF5 has no missing values of its own: an array
of floats uses NaN, and an array of integers a value that stands for missing,
which an attribute names ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-missing)).

Every dataset has a fill value, 0 by default, and the parts of a dataset that
were never written read as the fill value, without an error. A dataset that is
created at its full size and filled day by day reads as zeros wherever the
writing stopped or skipped a day ([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-loud)).
Give datasets of floats the fill value NaN, so that what was never written
reads as missing.


## One file, one writer {#sec-one-writer}

One program at a time writes an HDF5 file. While a program has a file open for
writing, HDF5 locks it, and any other program that opens it fails, even only to
read it. Many processes that write results, such as the jobs of a Slurm array,
write a file each, to be merged afterwards, or write [Zarr](zarr.qmd).
Parallel HDF5 lets processes of one MPI program write one file together.

HDF5 keeps parts of the index in memory and writes them when the file is
closed. A program that is killed while it writes, such as a job that exceeds
its time limit, can leave a file that does not open at all, with every dataset
in it, including those written long before. Close files with `with` in Python,
and write to a temporary file that is renamed only after it was closed
([](../../principles/design.qmd#sec-all-or-nothing)).

Unlike a Parquet file, a dataset can grow, along the axes that were declared
resizable when it was created, such as time. A deleted dataset leaves its space
behind: the file does not shrink, and `h5repack` copies it without the gaps.


# Working with HDF5 {#sec-usage}

The libraries read and write slices of datasets as arrays of the language, and
the command-line tools show what a file holds without a program.


## Write and read with h5py {#sec-h5py}

```python
import h5py
import numpy as np

with h5py.File("ocean.h5", "w") as f:
    temperature = f.create_dataset(
        "temperature", shape=(365, 720, 1440), dtype="float32",
        chunks=(1, 720, 1440), compression="gzip", fillvalue=np.nan,
    )
    temperature.attrs["units"] = "degC"
    temperature.attrs["axes"] = ["time", "lat", "lon"]
    temperature[0] = first_day             # writes one chunk

with h5py.File("ocean.h5", "r") as f:
    first_day = f["temperature"][0]        # reads one chunk
    everything = f["temperature"][()]      # reads the whole dataset
```

`f["temperature"]` is not an array but a handle to the dataset, valid while the
file is open: indexing it reads or writes only the chunks of the slice, as a
NumPy array, and `[()]` reads the whole dataset. Mode `"w"` replaces an
existing file, `"a"` opens one to change it. `f.create_group("run_01")` makes a
group, and paths such as `f["run_01/temperature"]` reach into it.
`maxshape=(None, 720, 1440)` makes the first axis resizable, and `resize` grows
it. Compress with `gzip`, which every HDF5 library reads; other compressions,
such as `lzf` or zstd, need a plugin in every program that reads the file.


## Read in R {#sec-r}

```r
library(rhdf5)

h5ls("ocean.h5")
first_day <- h5read("ocean.h5", "temperature", index = list(NULL, NULL, 1))
h5readAttributes("ocean.h5", "temperature")
```

The axes are reversed (@sec-axis-order): time is the last axis in R, so the
first day is `index = list(NULL, NULL, 1)`, although the attribute `axes` still
reads `time`, `lat`, `lon`. hdf5r, on CRAN, reverses the axes in the same way.


## Named axes with NetCDF-4 and xarray {#sec-netcdf}

```python
import xarray as xr

ocean = xr.open_dataset("ocean.nc")    # reads values only when used
first_june = ocean["temperature"].sel(time="2024-06-01")
first_june.to_netcdf("first_june.nc")
```

NetCDF-4 is HDF5 with conventions: every axis has a name and may have
coordinates, such as the dates of the time axis, and the attributes follow the
CF conventions, such as `units` and `_FillValue`. Readers in every language
understand them, and xarray in Python selects by the name of an axis and by
coordinate, such as a date, instead of by position, which removes the trap of
@sec-axis-order. For arrays on a grid, NetCDF-4 through xarray is usually a
better choice than plain HDF5. A NetCDF-4 file is still an HDF5 file, and h5py
and the command-line tools open it.


## Look inside a file {#sec-inspect}

```bash
h5ls -r ocean.h5                            # its groups and datasets
h5dump -H ocean.h5                          # with types and attributes
h5dump -H -p -d temperature ocean.h5        # with chunks and compression
h5repack ocean.h5 packed.h5                 # a copy without unused space
h5repack -l temperature:CHUNK=365x10x10 ocean.h5 series.h5   # other chunks
```

The command-line tools come with HDF5, in packages such as `hdf5-tools` of
Debian and Ubuntu, and HDFView shows a file in a window. `h5dump` without `-H`
prints the values as well, which for a large dataset is more than anyone wants
to read.
